newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, Japan leaders to discuss hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru, Japan leaders to discuss hostage crisis.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto agreed on Wednesday to an urgent meeting this weekend in Canada to try to break the deadlock in the 6-week-old Peruvian hostage crisis.

The meeting in Toronto at 10 a.m. (1500 GMT) on Saturday is a sign of growing concern in Lima and Tokyo that the 43-day siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru could drag on and endanger the lives of the 72 hostages held by Marxist rebels.
"President Fujimori has told us he wants to discuss the Peruvian situation with me as soon as possible," Hashimoto told reporters in Japan.

"I can't go into details at this delicate stage but what we must confirm is that we must not cave in to terrorism and at the same time seek the release of all captives unharmed and as soon as possible," he told a parliamentary committee later.
About two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats, including Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, were being held captive by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.

"In the planned meeting aspects of the strategy set out to reach a solution to the takeover of the residence will be evaluated jointly," Peru's chief crisis negotiator Domingo Palermo told a news conference.
Canada would host the talks because of its mediating role in the crisis which has been accepted by both sides, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said.
Hashimoto telephoned Fujimori on Tuesday to express concern that Peru was taking chances with the hostages' lives by stepping up psychological pressure on the estimated 15 guerrillas.

Scores of police took part in a massive show of force in front of the compound on Monday, driving past in an armoured convoy to the tune of marching music. Some made obscene gestures, provoking a burst a gunfire from the rebels which narrowly missed policemen aboard one vehicle.
Police blared their military tunes at the residence early on Wednesday and again in the evening moments after Red Cross workers had left the site.

The recent police activity around the diplomatic mansion has led some analysts in Lima to speculate that Fujimori was preparing an assault on the building. But government sources denied that was the purpose of Saturday's meeting.

"He will not meet with Hashimoto to apologise for the police attitude nor is he going to Canada to ask permission (from Japan) to enter the residence (by force)," a senior government official told Reuters.
The official, who requested anonymity, added that Fujimori would travel to Washington after the Toronto meeting "to thank President Clinton for his support."

In a flying visit to La Paz, Bolivia, last Thursday, Fujimori discussed the crisis with Bolivian President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada. Bolivia's ambassador in Lima Jorge Gumucio is the only non-Peruvian or Japanese still held captive.
Efforts to start talks with the MRTA guerrillas have stalled over the main rebel demand of freedom for about 400 jailed comrades, which Fujimori has refused to discuss.
The MRTA rebels originally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed a garden party at the residence Dec. 17.
They released most of the captives but kept those they consider the most important bargaining chips.

Aid workers and police say that most hostages are being treated for such conditions as hypertension, digestive ailments or depression. Red Cross workers took a stretcher and other medical supplies into the building on Wednesday as part of a drive to improve medical attention for the captives.
